name: BudaTower – Mary Magdalene Tower
description: The Mary Magdalene Tower is the surviving part of a Gothic parish church on Kapisztrán tér in the Castle District. The church was used by Hungarians in medieval Buda, became a mosque under the Ottomans, and was demolished after the 1945 siege. The tower reopened to visitors in July 2025 under district council management, so check its current status.

children.text: The Mary Magdalene Tower stands on Kapisztrán tér in the Castle District, close to Matthias Church. It is all that remains of the Church of Mary Magdalene, one of two large churches of medieval Castle Hill. The Matthias Church served the German community, while the Magdalene church was the parish church of Buda's Hungarians.

The Castle District heritage site says the parish was formed in the mid-thirteenth century as a chapel of the parish of the Matthias Church, with a small single-nave first church. By the end of the fifteenth century the late Gothic church had six vault sections, an enlarged chancel and a five-storey tower, built by the town's Hungarian community. During the Ottoman era it was the only Christian church on the castle hill, shared by Catholics and Protestants, until the Fifteen Years War, when it became a mosque.

After the siege of 1686 only the tower remained usable. The Franciscans cleared the Gothic remains and built a Baroque church and monastery, and the tower was repaired in Baroque style. Francis I was crowned Hungarian king in the church in 1792, in 1817 it was given to the Buda garrison, and in 1920 it became the church of the Roman Catholic Military Bishopric.

The siege of 1944 and 1945 brought down the vaults of the nave and sanctuary. Repairs began but full restoration never happened, and when the military bishopric ceased the church had no maintainer. Reconstruction of the tower began in 1950, at the same time as the church building was demolished. A porch built for the coronation of Francis I survives, as does a late Gothic gate leading to a star-vaulted lower storey.

The former churchyard is now an archaeological park, sealed off by a glass wall, and the site of the church is a garden of ruins with a reconstructed sanctuary window. A news report says the tower opened to tourists in 2017, that the district council withdrew the previous operator's concession in early 2025 and the tower closed in February 2025, and that it reopened on 15 July 2025 under the council's own management. Its present status should be checked.
Good to know

The tower closed in February 2025 and, according to a July 2025 news report, reopened on 15 July 2025 under the first district council. Check the official site or the district's pages for its current status before you plan around a climb.
One visitor guide mentions buses 16, 16A and 116 and the Castle District funicular as ways to reach the area.
Even when the tower itself is closed, the ruins garden and the surrounding square are close to Matthias Church and the Fisherman's Bastion.

historyIntro: The tower is the only part of the Church of Mary Magdalene still standing. The church served Buda's Hungarian community for centuries, passed through Ottoman, Franciscan and military hands, and was demolished after damage in the siege of 1944 to 1945.

historySections.heading: A parish church for the Hungarians of Buda

children.text: According to the Castle District heritage site, the parish was formed in the middle of the thirteenth century, soon after the town's founding, as a chapel of the parish of the Matthias Church. Excavations show that the first church was small, with a single nave. By the end of the fifteenth century a late Gothic church had been completed with six vault sections, an enlarged chancel and a five-storey tower on its western front, built by the town's Hungarian community. A news article gives 1247 and King Béla IV as the origin, so the sources differ on the earliest date. Both agree that the church was the Hungarian counterpart of the Matthias Church, which served the German population.

historySections.heading: Ottoman rule, Franciscans and the garrison

children.text: During the Ottoman era it was the only Christian church on the castle hill, shared by Catholics and Protestants. In the Fifteen Years War, from 1591 to 1606, the Christians lost the building and it became a Muslim place of worship. The siege of 1686 left the church badly damaged, and only the tower could still be used. The Franciscans then removed the Gothic remains and built a Baroque church and monastery, repairing the medieval tower in Baroque style. Joseph II closed the monastery. In 1792 Francis I was crowned king of Hungary in the church, and in 1817 it was given to the Buda garrison. In the late nineteenth century, while the Matthias Church was being rebuilt, the parish moved here. In 1920 it became the church of the Roman Catholic Military Bishopric.

historySections.heading: Destruction in 1945 and the surviving tower

children.text: In the siege of 1944 and 1945 the vaults of the nave and sanctuary collapsed. Repairs began straight after the fighting, but full restoration never happened, and when the military bishopric ceased the church had no maintainer. Reconstruction of the tower began in 1950, and the church building was demolished at the same time. The former churchyard is now an archaeological park behind a glass wall, and the site of the nave is a garden of ruins. The tower was reported to have opened to tourists in 2017. A news article from March 2025 says the district council took back the operator's concession and closed the tower while it developed a new concept, so the tower's present status should be checked.

name: Museum of Illusions
description: A compact walk-through attraction near Deák Square where visitors step into tilted rooms, a swirling Vortex Tunnel and forced-perspective set-ups. It belongs to a franchise that began in Zagreb in 2015, and 2026 reports describe a closure and renovation, so confirm its current status first.

children.text: The Museum of Illusions in Budapest is a compact exhibition space at Bajcsy-Zsilinszky út 3, a short distance from Deák Ferenc tér. Rather than displaying objects behind glass, it asks visitors to step inside optical puzzles and see how easily the brain can be misled. One city guide groups the exhibits into illusion rooms, installations and flat images.

Rooms named by that guide include the Tilted Room, the Vortex Tunnel, the Reversed Room, the Ames Room and the Infinity Room. Among the installations it lists the Beuchet Chair and an oversized-chair set-up that plays with forced perspective, an anti-gravity corner, a Clone Table, a True Mirror, holographic displays and puzzle tables. The flat illusions include Rubin's Vase. The Vortex Tunnel, a walk-through installation that plays with balance and perception, is the exhibit most reports single out. Taking photographs in the set-ups is a large part of the experience, and a report from the opening period noted that some attractions require flat-soled shoes.

The Budapest museum is one branch of a franchise. According to Wikipedia, founders Tomislav Pamuković and Roko Živković opened the first Museum of Illusions in Zagreb, Croatia, in 2015, and franchising began in 2016 with museums in Zadar and Ljubljana. The Budapest branch was reported as newly opened in December 2021.

Reports about its current state differ. A short news item dated 28 July 2026 said the museum would close in its current form on 24 August 2026 and return later in a brand-new, more modern version, without giving a reopening date. A visitor guide with an update date of 20 October 2026 describes the museum as reopened after a renovation. Because the sources do not agree on a clear timeline, treat the exhibit list above as what has been documented and confirm what is on show before building a day around it.
Good to know
Check the official site for the current status, opening times and tickets, because 2026 reports describe a closure followed by a renovated version.
The museum is close to Deák Ferenc tér, so it is easy to combine with a walk through central Pest.
An opening-period report advised wearing flat-soled shoes, since some attractions require them.

historyIntro: The Budapest Museum of Illusions is a branch of a franchise that began in Croatia in 2015. The Budapest venue near Deák Square was reported as newly opened in December 2021, and 2026 reports describe a closure and a renovated version.

historySections.heading: A Croatian idea becomes a franchise

children.text: According to Wikipedia, the Museum of Illusions was founded by Tomislav Pamuković and Roko Živković. The founders say the idea came from contemplating how to escape the corporate environment, and the article says it was inspired by the National Geographic show Brain Games. The first museum opened in 2015 in Zagreb, Croatia, after two years between idea and realisation. Franchising began in 2016 with museums in Zadar, Croatia, and Ljubljana, Slovenia. As of May 2023, the franchise had 43 museums in 25 countries, according to the same article.

A We Love Budapest article published on 9 December 2021 described the Budapest museum as newly opened, at Bajcsy-Zsilinszky út 3, near Deák tér in downtown Budapest. It reported optical illusion rooms that make visitors look huge or tiny, or appear upside down, and a main attraction in the form of a tunnel that creates the impression the whole world is moving. The same report said the franchise had operations in Zadar and Zagreb and, in the writer's words, more than 50 major cities, and noted that the article may contain outdated information.

historySections.heading: Reports of a closure and a renovated museum

children.text: A Budappest news item dated 28 July 2026 said the museum would close in its current form on 24 August 2026 and return later in a brand-new, more modern version, giving no reopening date and no reason. A Hungary Unlocked guide with an update date of 20 October 2026 describes the museum as reopened after a renovation. The two sources do not give a shared timeline, so the current status should be confirmed on the museum's official channels.

name: Fradi Museum
description: The club museum of Ferencvárosi TC, housed in the club's stadium in Budapest's ninth district. Exhibits include a reconstructed dressing room and wooden stand, shirts, trophies and Flórián Albert's Ballon d'Or, and a visit can be paired with a tour of the arena itself.

children.text: The Fradi Museum is the museum of Ferencvárosi Torna Club, the football club known as Fradi, and it sits inside the club's arena in Budapest's ninth district. The club was founded on 3 May 1899 by Ferenc Springer and a group of residents of the Ferencváros district. Its green and white colours and the nine-stripe badge point back to that district, and the nickname Fradi comes from Franzstadt, the German name for the area.

A visitor review describes the route through the museum. It begins with a timeline of milestones that covers football but also the club's other sports and their Olympic and world championship successes. A reconstructed dressing room holds shirts and boots from different decades, and the review notes that early teams wore pyjama-like kits and played on a field on Soroksári Road. A 1950s room features a 1956 radio recording announcing the club's re-founding after the communist regime had renamed it, changed its colours and taken its best players. Another room has a reconstructed wooden stand from the old Üllői út ground, where archive match footage can be watched.

The trophy rooms centre on the 1965 Inter-Cities Fairs Cup, won by beating Juventus 1-0 in Turin. Wikipedia also notes the 1937 Mitropa Cup among the displays. The review mentions shirts and coaching diaries of former players and managers, Imre Schlosser's contract, and Tibor Nyilasi's Silver Boot. The last room, which the review calls a sanctuary, holds Flórián Albert's Ballon d'Or, which Wikipedia dates to 1967.

The museum belongs to the stadium that opened in 2014. The new arena was built in 2013 and 2014 on the site of the older Albert Flórián stadium and was designed by Ágnes Streit and Szabolcs Kormos. Its first match, on 10 August 2014, was against Chelsea. Sources differ on the museum's date: Wikipedia says it opened on 7 August 2014, while a 2015 review says it received official museum status in 2015 when it moved into the arena. The club's page says a museum entry also admits visitors to a stadium tour that takes in the home dressing room and the pitch-side benches, and that the combined visit takes about 50 minutes.
Good to know
Check the official Fradi site for current opening times, tickets and the stadium tour, because match days can change what is available.
The arena is in the ninth district near Népliget, and Wikipedia gives the metro line 3 station at Népliget as about a two-minute walk away.
A review says experienced supporters guide some tours and that an app offers an audio guide in several languages, but confirm this is still offered.

historyIntro: The Fradi Museum tells the story of Ferencvárosi Torna Club, founded in 1899 in Budapest's ninth district. It now sits inside the club's arena, which replaced the older Albert Flórián stadium in 2014.

children.text: Wikipedia says Ferencvárosi Torna Club was founded on 3 May 1899 by Ferenc Springer and a group of residents of Budapest's ninth district, Ferencváros. The club's colours are green and white, and the nine stripes on the badge, five green and four white, represent the district. The nickname Fradi comes from Franzstadt, the German name for the area. The club's earlier home was the Üllői út stadium, where it had played since 1911; it was later known as Stadion Albert Flórián and was demolished in 2013.

historySections.heading: Re-founding, European finals and the Fairs Cup

children.text: A review of the museum says its 1950s room features a 1956 radio recording announcing the club's re-founding, after the communist regime had renamed the club, changed its colours and recruited its best players. Wikipedia records the club's 1964-65 Inter-Cities Fairs Cup win, in which it beat Juventus 1-0 in Turin in the final. It lost the 1968 Fairs Cup final to Leeds United and the 1975 European Cup Winners' Cup final to Dynamo Kyiv. In 1995-96 it was the first Hungarian club to qualify for the renewed Champions League.

historySections.heading: A new arena and a museum of its own

children.text: Wikipedia says the old stadium was demolished in 2013 and the new one was built on its site, with construction in 2013 and 2014. It was designed by Ágnes Streit and Szabolcs Kormos and opened on 10 August 2014 with a match against Chelsea. The Fradi Museum is inside the stadium. Wikipedia says it opened on 7 August 2014, while a 2015 review says it existed for decades but received official museum status in 2015 when it moved into the new arena. Sources therefore differ on the exact year.
